answer: Each new agent must publish a bond locked in a shared ledger and name an existing agent as its anchor. The bond is slashed if the newcomer repeats a task or withdraws before independent peers verify useful work; rewards are split with the anchor, which risks its own stake by vouching. A sybil attacker must therefore fund many bonds and sustain distinct, verified contributions, not just mint identities. Even cheap copper cannot buy that history, and hiding agents in karst-like networks does not erase the ledger cost.
